title: Evaluating the Effect of Teachers' Group Performance Incentives on Pupil Achievement
research_question: Do monetary performance bonuses paid to teachers, tied to their students' scholastic outcomes, causally improve pupil achievement and reduce dropout rates? How does the effectiveness and cost-efficiency of such pay-for-performance compare to providing schools with additional teaching resources and on-the-job teacher training aimed at the same outcomes?
data_description: Data were provided by Israel's Ministry of Education and cover the academic years 1993-1997, comprising two pre-program years (1993-1994) and two full implementation years (1996-1997), with additional coverage through 1998 for the resources program. The data form a school-level panel constructed from micro student files containing achievement measures (number of credit units earned, average matriculation score, science credit units, proportions taking matriculation exams and earning matriculation certificates) and student characteristics (gender, parental schooling, family size, immigration status). Student identification numbers permit tracking dropout rates from grades 9 through 12. School files include school size, number of teachers, boarding facilities, and teacher characteristics (age, experience, education) for 1997. The unit of observation is the secondary school (and individual students within schools), covering Israel's roughly 320 high schools, of which 170 are comprehensive secondary schools serving grades 7-12.
institutional_context: In February 1995 Israel's Ministry of Education launched an experimental tournament-style program in 62 secondary comprehensive schools, awarding about $1.44 million in monetary bonuses to the top one-third of schools ranked on improvements in average credit units, share entering the matriculation track, share earning matriculation certificates, and dropout rates. About 75% of each award was distributed to teachers as salary bonuses (proportional to gross income) and the remainder funded teacher facilities; bonuses ranged from $200 to $715 per teacher. Eligibility required being a secondary comprehensive school and the only school of its type (secular Hebrew, religious boys', religious girls', or Arab) within its community. Simultaneously, the Ministry ran a parallel three-year program endowing 22 schools (selected from 70-75 applicants) with roughly 30-50 additional weekly teaching hours and 8 monthly hours of on-the-job teacher training, costing about $1.13-1.15 million annually.
